content.thinking:
This narrative framing from a climate scientist stresses self-correction, humility, and openness to feedback rather than pushing a message, which speaks directly to trust dimensions like openness and integrity and counters the "biased scientist" concern. Though it's a bit dry and academic, the interview format helps, though mentioning model uncertainty could slightly soften perceived competence.

I'm estimating moderate gains across the trust metrics—openness moving most (~2.3), with smaller bumps to trust_post (~1.3) and distrust dropping around -1.0. Funding perceptions get a modest lift (+1.2) from the call for further research, policy role and institutional trust nudge up slightly (+0.7, +0.6), and belief, concern, and policy/behavior measures each tick up marginally (+0.3 to +0.5), with donation to AMS barely moving.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is a first-person narrative from a working climate scientist that directly targets the openness and integrity dimensions of trust: self-questioning, admitting model errors, explicitly disavowing any agenda ('not to push for a certain message'), and framing science as collective self-correction. That maps almost perfectly onto the multidimensional trust battery (especially openness-to-feedback and honesty items), and narrative/interview formats carry a small immediate warmth/trust advantage over expository text, so I place it slightly above the expected arm average on the primary outcome (~+2.4, d≈0.10). It is anchored downward on trust_post and belief_post because those were asked pre-treatment, and its explicit emphasis on residual uncertainty ('we still do not fully understand regional trends') caps any gain in belief certainty and concern, which get only fractional-point effects. The mention that further research is required gives a modest lift to funding_perceptions; the 'best possible information for decision makers' line supports the communication/involvement items but the anti-advocacy stance mutes the advocacy item, so policy_role gets under a point. Distal policy support and behavioral intentions get ~0.25 fffff0.35 points, and incentivized outcomes near zero (a few cents to the AMS, well under a percentage point on newsletter signup), consistent with megastudy evidence that attitude shifts rarely propagate to costly behavior.
